papers.title_in_file: Classification with Quantum Machine Learning: A Survey
papers.what_it_is: A literature survey of about 30 quantum machine learning classification works, sorted into QML, quantum-inspired and hybrid quantum-classical approaches, with a proposed classification pipeline, a note on data encodings and subroutines, and a list of challenges.

existing.note: The conclusion says this. The survey's own Table 2 also lists limitations of the same algorithms (for example, one row states that the classifier does not achieve better performance with some data), so the blanket statement is a summary of cited works, not a result of the survey. The conclusion is on page 13 of the text layer.
quotes: QML algorithms outperformed classical ML in performance and speed up.

existing.note: The sentence is in the Encoding methods challenge (Sec. 5, text p.12-13). The paper cites reference 74 (a D-Wave slide deck) for it.
existing.anchor: Sec. 5, item 2, Encoding methods, text p.12-13
quotes: Encoding data to quantum states is one of QML challenges, this process takes high consumption time and power for mapping from classical data into quantum data

existing.note: The paper adds a cited remark that researchers write algorithms for NISQ hardware that match the qubit count.

the big and key challenge is to build quantum computers with a large number of qubits to implement, test QML algorithms

existing.note: Both statements are in the abstract and in Sec. 2. The paper does not list the 30 works by count; Table 1 lists the works it covers.
quotes: we cover about 30 publications that are published lately in Quantum Machine Learning (QML)
into three approaches: QML, quantum-inspired ML, and Hybrid quantum-classical ML
existing.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and its own classification in the abstract and in Sec. 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the aim of the paper is a comprehensive survey of the state-of-the-art advances in quantum machine learning, with the recent QML classification works as the main focus.
quotes: The aim of this paper presents and summarizes a comprehensive survey of the state-of-the-art advances in Quantum Machine Learning (QML).
Especially, recent QML classification works.
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the survey's own aim and scope.

assertions.value: The authors state that they base the split into approaches on whether the information processing device (the type of algorithm) is classical or quantum and whether the data are classical or quantum.
quotes: The classification of approaches based on information processing devices (a type of algorithm) is classical or quantum and type of data are classical or quantum
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 2 states the criterion the survey uses to sort the works.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey gives no rule that decides every case; the paper lists reference 33 (a quantum decision tree) in Table 1 and, in Sec. 3d, names it as a hybrid classifier, so a work's label may differ between places.

assertions.value: The authors report that Rebentrost et al. presented a quantum version of the support vector machine (QSVM) for classification of big data, and state that QSVM achieved logarithmic speed up over classical counterparts.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 1, text p.2; Sec. 2A, text p.3
quotes: QSVM achieved logarithmic speed up over classical counterparts.
QSVM is a big data binary classifier.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (reference 24); the survey does not test it and does not give the conditions of the speed up.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey drops the conditions of the original result (for example the data access assumptions); no condition is quoted here.

assertions.value: The authors state that a cited work implemented a support vector machine on a quantum annealer device (DW2000Q) and call it QA-SVM.
quotes: implemented SVM on quantum annealer device (23) (DW2000Q) called QA-SVM.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of other work (reference 22).
assertions.reader_inference: The survey writes Dennis, et al. for this work. Reference 22 is Willsch, Willsch, De Raedt and Michielsen, so Dennis is a given name used as a surname.

assertions.value: The authors state that Sergioli et al. proposed a binary quantum-inspired classifier based on the formalism of quantum theory, and that it achieved a higher performance compared with different classical models.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 1, text p.2; Sec. 2B, text p.3
quotes: this classifier achieved a higher performance compared with different classical models.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (reference 28); no data are given here.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 of the survey lists this classifier with the limitation that it does not work efficiently with many feature vectors in a large data set, so the higher performance has a stated limit in the same paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Nearest Mean Classifier (QNMC) achieved higher accuracy than the classical counterpart (NMC) in many medical data sets, exclusively on a cancer data set.
quotes: The algorithm achieved higher accuracy in many medical data sets than the classical counterpart (NMC) exclusively cancer data set.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (reference 30).
assertions.reader_inference: Table 2 lists for this row the limitation that it does not achieve better performance with one of its data sets; the sentence in Sec. 2B and the table are not fully consistent about where QNMC wins.

assertions.value: The authors state that a quantum K-nearest-neighbour algorithm based on the hamming distance (Ruan et al.) outperforms Centroid and QNN on time performance and classification accuracy.
quotes: QKNN outperforms Centroid and QNN on time performance and classification accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (reference 44).
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence does not say whether the comparison is run on a quantum device, on a simulator, or by a cost count.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hybrid quantum feature selection algorithm (HQFSA) accomplished quadratic time complexity and better performance in some of the cases, and that its main disadvantage is that it runs on a quantum simulator only.
quotes: The proposed algorithm accomplished quadratic time complexity and better performance in some of the cases.
The main disadvantage of HQFSA is running on a quantum simulator only.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result and a limit the survey attributes to other work (reference 39).

assertions.value: The survey's comparison table of QML classifiers lists, for the variational quantum classifier row, the advantage 'Higher performance' and the limitation 'High cost', and for the QSVM row the limitation 'Difficult implementation' beside the advantage 'Better accuracy from classical SVM'.
assertions.anchor: Table 2, text p.6 (the text layer interleaves the columns; rows read from the row labels)
quotes: Breast Higher performance High cost
Breast Better accuracy from Difficult implementation
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 2 summarizes cited works and gives no measurement of its own.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer breaks the table columns apart, so the pairing of an advantage with a limitation rests on the order of rows; the table image should be checked by the coordinator.

assertions.value: The survey's comparison table of QML classifiers states for the autonomous perceptron model (APM) row the limitation that it works on a classical computer only.
quotes: Work on classical computer
assertions.certainty_reason: Table 2 summarizes a cited work.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote is only 25 characters and the text layer cuts the rest ('only.') onto a later line; the column pairing needs the table image.

assertions.value: The authors state that any quantum algorithm, or a classical algorithm implemented on a quantum computer, consists of three main phases: encoding, quantum computation, and decoding.
quotes: a quantum computer or in general any quantum algorithm consists of the main three phases (13, 14): encoding,
assertions.certainty_reason: A framing statement the survey supports by citation (references 13 and 14); not tested.

assertions.value: The authors define basis encoding as the simplest method to encode data to quantum data, associating an n-bit classical input with the computational basis of an n-qubit input.
quotes: Basis Encoding is the simplest method to encode data to quantum data.
This method associates between n-bit
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3b defines the encoding that the survey describes.

assertions.value: The authors state that amplitude encoding is the most used and popular encoding method in QML algorithms, and that it associates classical data with quantum state amplitudes after the classical vector is normalized.
quotes: Amplitude Encoding is the most used and popular method encoding in QML algorithms is amplitude encoding.
The main idea of amplitude encoding based on association classical data with quantum state amplitudes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A popularity statement with no count or citation given; the definition part is not the claim.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no survey count behind most used. Only two encodings are outlined; the paper refers the reader to other sources for the rest.

assertions.value: The authors state that variational quantum circuits are also known as parameterized quantum circuits, that most hybrid quantum-classical algorithms rely on them, and that they consist of two phases: a quantum phase and a classical phase.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 3c, text p.7; Figure 1, text p.8
quotes: Variational quantum circuits also known as parameterized quantum circuits, most hybrid quantum-classical algorithms rely on these circuits (51).
variational quantum circuits consist of two phases (see Figure 1): the quantum phase and classical phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3c defines the variational circuit as the survey uses it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the key idea of the variational circuit is optimizing the parameters according to an objective function, and that the circuit can be optimized by classical algorithms such as gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and particle swarm optimization.
quotes: The key idea of the variational circuit is optimizing the parameters according to an objective function.
can be optimized by classical optimization algorithms as gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent and particle swarm optimization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3c describes the circuit's method as the survey defines it.

assertions.value: The authors propose a quantum classification scheme of six phases: collect datasets, pre-processing and encoding, training, validation, testing, and decoding.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 3d, text p.7; Figure 2, text p.9
quotes: We propose a new a quantum classification scheme consists of six phases as collect datasets, pre-processing & encoding, training, validation (evaluate and optimize model), testing phase and decoding phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3d defines the scheme that the survey proposes.
assertions.reader_inference: The scheme is a pipeline description. The survey reports no test of it on any data.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the pre-processing and encoding phase the number of features is reduced to be compatible with the limited number of qubits available on a quantum device, and the data are split into training, validation and test sets.
quotes: reduce number of the features to are compatible with available limited numbers of qubits on quantum device and split data to training, validation and test set.
assertions.certainty_reason: Sec. 3d describes a step of the proposed scheme.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML is pursued to solve challenges that still exist in classical machine learning, and that with the growing size of data the training time and memory consumption of the learning phase increase.
quotes: To solve challenges and difficult tasks that still exist in classical machine learning.
With increasing size of data, learning phase training time and memory consumption to increase during the learning phase.
assertions.certainty_reason: A motivation stated without evidence in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that Shor's algorithm solves factorization with exponential speedup and Grover's algorithm searches unstructured data with a quadratic speedup.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 4, text p.9; Table 3, text p.10
quotes: Shor’s algorithm for solving factorization problems with exponential speedup, Grover’s algorithm search problem in unstructured data with a quadratic speedup
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the survey attributes to other work (references 8 and 9); stated without conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: Both results are well known and proved in the cited papers; the survey gives no conditions (for example, the oracle model for Grover's quadratic speedup).

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problem is an NP-hard problem that is hard for classical hardware and algorithms, and that it is solved by quantum annealing.
quotes: Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization problem is NP-hard problems that are hard to the classical hardware and algorithms solve it.
QUBO problem is solved by quantum annealing(57)
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the survey supports by citation only; no result is shown.
assertions.reader_inference: The sentence does not say that annealing beats classical solvers on QUBO; it says the problem is solved by annealing. No speedup is claimed in Table 3 (the speed up cell is a dash).

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Dunjko et al., that quantum machine learning can improve in run-time and efficiency.
quotes: According to Dunjko, V et al. (15) Quantum ML can improve in run-time and efficiency.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement attributed to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that D-Wave introduced Quadrant algorithms, based on CPUs, GPUs and a quantum annealing computer, and that Quadrant ML algorithms can achieve more performance with low-cost training data with large data over classical deep learning and traditional algorithms.
quotes: D-wave introduced Quadrant algorithms based on Central Processing Unit (CPU), Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) and Quantum annealing computer.
Quadrant ML algorithms can achieve more performance with low-cost training data with large data over classical deep learning and traditional algorithms (61) (62).
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor performance claim relayed by the survey from a press release and a paper (references 61 and 62); no data are shown.
assertions.reader_inference: Reference 62 is a D-Wave press release, so the claim is the vendor's own. The survey does not say what benchmark supports it.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum computing can boost traditional algorithms by two methods: implementing classical algorithms on quantum computers or simulators, which needs the classical data to be encoded into quantum data, and building QML algorithms from quantum algorithms or subroutines.
quotes: Quantum computing can boost traditional algorithms by two different methods
This method needs to encode classical data into quantum data.
assertions.certainty_reason: A framing statement; no test in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Fourier Transform is a quantum version of the inverse discrete Fourier Transform and that QFT achieves exponential speed-up.
quotes: Quantum Fourier Transform is a quantum version of inverse discrete Fourier
QFT achieves exponential speed-up.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement supported by citation (reference 64) with no conditions.
assertions.reader_inference: The usual statement is that the QFT is the quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform, with a speedup over the classical FFT only for a quantum-state input and output. The survey's wording (inverse) and the unconditioned speed-up should be checked against its source before the grade is set.

assertions.value: The authors note from their table of quantum subroutines that the quantum Fourier transform and the variational quantum circuit are the most common and used subroutines in most algorithms and applications.
quotes: We note that quantum Fourier transform (QFT) and variational quantum circuit is the most common and used subroutines in most algorithms and applications.
assertions.certainty_reason: An observation from a table of about seven subroutines; the table is not a count of use in the surveyed works.
assertions.reader_inference: Table 4 maps subroutines to applications and references but does not count how many surveyed QML classifiers use each; the observation is not a measured frequency.

assertions.value: The authors report in the caption of its qubit-progress figure, citing its source there, that IBM achieved 50 qubits in 2017 and that Rigetti achieved 128 qubits in 2019.
quotes: IBM achieved in 2017, 50 qubits.
in 2019, Rigetti achieved 128 qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Figures taken from a secondary report (reference 75, an IDB publication).
assertions.reader_inference: The qubit counts are vendor-announced figures from a secondary report; a qubit count says nothing of gate quality, which the survey itself notes in the next assertion.

assertions.value: The authors state that increasing the number of qubits with a high error rate does not make a powerful quantum processor, and that a powerful processor with a low error rate will increase exponentially by increasing the number of quantum bits.
quotes: If numbers of qubits increase with a high error rate don’t make a powerful quantum processor (80).
Powerful quantum processer with a low error rate will increase exponentially by increasing numbers of quantum bits.
assertions.certainty_reason: A caveat the survey attributes to reference 80; no data are given.
assertions.reader_inference: The second sentence says power grows exponentially with qubit count at low error rate; the survey states no condition.

assertions.value: The authors state that researchers develop algorithms that work on small-scale NISQ hardware, that limited qubits lead to using fewer features and so to losing a lot of important data, and that with limited qubits big data processing cannot be applied on quantum devices.
quotes: limited qubits number using a less number of features that lead to losing a lot of important data
with limited qubits can’t apply big data processing on quantum devices (78, 79)
assertions.certainty_reason: A limit stated with citations (references 78 and 79); not tested in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that LaRose and Coyle applied several data encodings to the same data and showed that encoding techniques can improve the model accuracy of a binary quantum classifier.
quotes: applied several encoding data on the same data and showed that encoding data techniques can be improved the model accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (reference 81, an arXiv preprint at the time).

assertions.value: The authors state that they think researchers will develop, in the near future, new theoretical and applied ML algorithms compatible with the available quantum hardware, including new classification techniques based on the variational circuit that reduce the circuit depth.
quotes: In near future, we think that researchers will develop new theoretical and applied ML algorithms that are compatible with available quantum hardware.
working on reducing the depth of quantum circuit.
assertions.certainty_reason: A prediction stated by the authors, with no support.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML techniques are more effective than traditional machine learning in many real-world applications in speedup and accuracy, and list among them big data classification, spam detection, medical applications and image classification.
quotes: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) techniques are more effective in many real-world applications comparable to traditional machine learning in speedup and accuracy
assertions.certainty_reason: An author's claim; Sec. 6 lists applications with citations but shows no comparison.
assertions.reader_inference: Sec. 3 and Table 2 report that several of these classifiers run on a simulator or on classical hardware only, so no real-world advantage is shown on quantum hardware in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as future work, they will apply quantum-inspired and hybrid quantum-classical algorithms on real-world data to compare their performance.
quotes: Our future work, we will apply quantum-inspired and hybrid quantum-classical algorithm on real-world data to compare its performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: The conclusion states what the survey has not done: it runs no performance comparison of its own.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey is a literature review with no experiments of its own, so every performance statement in it is a report of cited work.
